Which measure of center and spread is most appropriate to report for this distribution, and why?

Choices:
A. Mean and standard deviation, because they use every data value in the distribution.
B. Mean and range, because the range captures the full spread including the long visits.
C. Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the strong right skew and the high outlier.
D. Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant but the shape of the distribution doesn't affect measures of spread.

choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use every data value in the distribution.
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Both the mean and standard deviation are pulled toward the long right tail and the high outlier (65); they are not resistant, so 'uses every value' is not a reason to prefer them for a skewed distribution.

choices.text: Mean and range, because the range captures the full spread including the long visits.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The range is determined entirely by the two most extreme values, making it even more sensitive to the outlier than the standard deviation; the mean is also not resistant.

choices.text: Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the strong right skew and the high outlier.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The median and IQR depend only on the middle portion of the ordered data, so they are not distorted by the skew or the outlier at 65 minutes -- the standard choice for a skewed distribution.

choices.text: Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant but the shape of the distribution doesn't affect measures of spread.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This mixes a resistant measure of center with a non-resistant measure of spread; shape and outliers affect standard deviation just as much as they affect the mean.

choices.rationale: Fatima's z-score is (640 - 500)/100 = 1.4. Diego's z-score is (26 - 20)/4 = 1.5. Standardizing puts both scores on the same scale, and Diego's is higher.

choices.text: Fatima, because 640 is a higher raw score than 26.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Comparing raw scores directly ignores that the two tests have completely different means and standard deviations; raw scores from different distributions are not comparable without standardizing.

choices.text: Fatima, because her raw score is farther from her test's mean (140 points) than Diego's is from his (6 points).
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Comparing raw point distances from the mean ignores the different scales (standard deviations) of the two tests; 140 points on a test with SD 100 is less extreme than 6 points on a test with SD 4.

choices.text: The two students performed identically, because both scored above their test's mean.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Both scoring above the mean does not mean the performances are equivalent; the magnitude of each score's standardized distance from the mean still needs to be compared.

A polling organization constructs a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of adults in a state who support a new transportation initiative and obtains the interval (0.46, 0.54) based on a random sample of 800 adults.

Which is a correct interpretation of this confidence interval?

Choices:
A. There is a 95% probability that the true population proportion is between 0.46 and 0.54.
B. 95% of adults in the state support the initiative, plus or minus 4 percentage points.
C. If this exact sample were surveyed 100 times, the sample proportion would fall between 0.46 and 0.54 ninety-five times.
D. We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.46 to 0.54 captures the true proportion of all adults in the state who support the initiative, based on the method used to construct it.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The true population proportion is a fixed (though unknown) number, not a random variable, so it is incorrect to assign a probability to it falling in a specific interval.

choices.text: 95% of adults in the state support the initiative, plus or minus 4 percentage points.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This confuses the confidence interval for the unknown population proportion with a statement about what fraction of individual adults support the initiative.

choices.text: If this exact sample were surveyed 100 times, the sample proportion would fall between 0.46 and 0.54 ninety-five times.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: "95% confidence" describes the long-run behavior of the method across many different random samples, not repeated surveys of the same fixed sample.

choices.text: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.46 to 0.54 captures the true proportion of all adults in the state who support the initiative, based on the method used to construct it.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This correctly ties the 95% confidence level to the reliability of the interval-construction method over repeated random sampling, rather than to a probability statement about the fixed parameter.

A nutritionist wants to construct a confidence interval for the mean sugar content (in grams) of a population of energy bars using a random sample of 8 bars. A dotplot of the 8 sample values shows a strong right skew with one bar much higher in sugar content than the rest.

Is it appropriate to construct a one-sample t-interval for the mean using this sample?

Choices:
A. No, because the sample size is small (n = 8) and the sample data show strong skewness, so there is no good reason to believe the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal.
B. Yes, because the sample was randomly selected, and random selection is the only condition required for a t-interval.
C. Yes, because the Central Limit Theorem guarantees the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal for any sample size greater than 5.
D. No, because t-intervals can never be used with sample sizes smaller than 30.

choices.text: No, because the sample size is small (n = 8) and the sample data show strong skewness, so there is no good reason to believe the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal.
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: With a small sample and clear skewness/an outlier in the data, there is no basis for assuming the population is approximately normal or that the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal, so the t-interval's normality condition is not satisfied.

choices.text: Yes, because the sample was randomly selected, and random selection is the only condition required for a t-interval.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Random selection is one condition, but the normal/large-sample condition on the shape of the data or the sampling distribution must also be checked; it is not the only requirement.

choices.text: Yes, because the Central Limit Theorem guarantees the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal for any sample size greater than 5.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: There is no such rule; the Central Limit Theorem's normal approximation improves gradually with sample size and depends on how skewed the population is, not a fixed cutoff of 5.

choices.text: No, because t-intervals can never be used with sample sizes smaller than 30.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This overgeneralizes a common rule of thumb into an absolute rule; small samples can still support a t-interval when there's good reason to believe the population itself is approximately normal, which is not the case here given the observed skew.

A researcher collects data on eye color (categorized as Brown, Blue, Green, Hazel, or Other) for a random sample of 60 people from a small town, wanting to test whether the town's eye-color distribution matches known national percentages. After computing expected counts under the national percentages, the expected count for the "Other" category is 2.4, while all other categories have expected counts above 10.

What is the best course of action given this situation?

Choices:
A. Proceed with the chi-square goodness-of-fit test as planned; expected counts do not need to meet any minimum threshold as long as the observed counts are all positive.
B. Combine the "Other" category with another sparse or conceptually similar category so that all expected counts are at least 5, then proceed with the chi-square goodness-of-fit test using the reduced set of categories.
C. Switch to a chi-square test for independence instead, since that test has no minimum expected-count requirement.
D. Increase the significance level from 0.05 to 0.10 to compensate for the small expected count in the "Other" category.

choices.text: Proceed with the chi-square goodness-of-fit test as planned; expected counts do not need to meet any minimum threshold as long as the observed counts are all positive.
choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Chi-square procedures require expected counts to meet a minimum threshold (commonly at least 5 in each category) for the chi-square approximation to be valid; observed counts being positive does not address this.

choices.text: Combine the "Other" category with another sparse or conceptually similar category so that all expected counts are at least 5, then proceed with the chi-square goodness-of-fit test using the reduced set of categories.
choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Combining categories to raise low expected counts to at least 5 is the standard way to satisfy the expected-counts condition while still allowing a valid chi-square goodness-of-fit test to proceed.

choices.text: Switch to a chi-square test for independence instead, since that test has no minimum expected-count requirement.
choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The expected-counts condition applies to chi-square procedures generally, including tests for independence and homogeneity; switching tests does not remove the requirement.

choices.text: Increase the significance level from 0.05 to 0.10 to compensate for the small expected count in the "Other" category.
choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Adjusting the significance level addresses the decision threshold, not the underlying condition violation caused by a too-small expected count; it does not fix the validity problem.
